It has one stressed syllable which always occupies the last position of a word as its nucleus, and it may have weakly stressed or unstressed syllables as its periphery. [...] A monosyllabic word contains a single syllable. It is formed by one major syllable which always takes a strong stress. [...] a) It is formed by one presyllable followed by one major syllable. new_statements.quote: The phonological word in Gong may have up to four syllables. It has one stressed syllable which always occupies the last position of a word as its nucleus, and it may have weakly stressed or unstressed syllables as its periphery. [...] a) It is formed by one presyllable followed by one major syllable. The structure of this type of disyllabic word carries no stress on the presyllable and carries strong stress on the major syllable (u.s) [...] Since stress in Gong can be predictable from the position of the stress in a word and from the syllable structure, it needs not be marked overtly at the phonemic level.
new_statements.citation: Mayuree Thawornpat. 2006. Gong: An endangered language of Thailand. PhD dissertation (Linguistics), Institute of Language and Culture for Rural Development, Mahidol University.
new_statements.locator: Chapter V, section 5.1.2 'Phonological word', pp. 95-97 (PDF pp. 111-113); cf. lit. review p. 21 (Pusit 1986) and p. 100
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (220 pp., text layer; extracted text of PDF p. 111 = printed p. 95). Section 5.1.2 'Phonological word' reads exactly as quoted: 'The phonological word in Gong may have up to four syllables. It has one stressed syllable which always occupies the last position of a word as its nucleus, and it may have weakly stressed or unstressed syllables as its periphery.' The disyllabic passage (p. 96: '..carries no stress on the presyllable and carries strong stress on the major syllable (u.s)..') and the closing sentence (p. 97: 'Since stress in Gong can be predictable from the position of the stress in a word and from the syllable structure, it needs not be marke…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the phonological word (the 'major syllable'); preceding presyllables are unstressed and 'minor syllables' carry weak stress, giving patterns S, u.s, w.s, w.u.s, u.w.s, u.w.u.s. Stress is predictable and non-contrastive in this tonal language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A three-way distinction strong/weak/unstressed is used: non-final 'minor syllables' (full syllables, e.g. first syllable of 'crocodile', 'dragonfly') carry weak stress, 'presyllables' (reduced Ca33 syllables) carry none; no rhythmic secondary-stress rule beyond this syllable-type distinction.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; stress said to be fully predictable. Only /i a u/ occur in open unstressed syllables (p. 100). Description restricted to elderly fluent speakers of Kok Chiang; younger speakers' phonology is Thai/Lao-assimilated.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (rank below the intonation group in a Pike-style hierarchy), illustrated with citation forms of mono- to tetrasyllabic words including compounds. The literature review (p. 21) reports the identical rule from Pusit (1986) for the Khok Khwai (Uthai Thani) dialect: 'A strongly stressed syllable always occupies the final position of the phonological word and functions as the nucleus of the word.' Bradley (cited p. 20) notes word/clause-level intonation with a terminal rise in emphatic speech, variably used in citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted first-hand description (Mayuree 2006 ch. V) is of the Kok Chiang village dialect (Dan Chang district, Suphanburi) as spoken by elderly fluent speakers; the same thesis (p. 21) reports the identical final-stress rule second-hand from Pusit (1986) for the Khok Khwai dialect (Uthai Thani). Both are varieties of Ugong/Gong, glottocode ugon1239 (ISO ugo); no separate dialect glottocodes.

sources.note: Ch. V sec. 5.1.2 'Phonological word' (pp. 95-97, Kok Chiang dialect): the phonological word (up to four syllables) has one stressed syllable which always occupies the last position of the word; presyllables carry no stress, minor syllables weak stress, the final major syllable strong stress (patterns S, u.s, w.s, w.u.s, u.w.s, u.w.u.s); stress is predictable and not marked. Lit. review p. 21 reports the same rule second-hand from Pusit (1986) for the Uthai Thani dialect. p.100: only /i a u/ occur in open unstressed syllables.

sources.note: The text says nothing about word stress, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's final-syllable rule (final stress) or the 2006 thesis statement. The transcription practice (primary stress marked on the final syllable of polysyllables, secondary on an initial syllable) is consistent with the catalog's final stress but is not a statement. Describes the Kok Chiang (Suphanburi) dialect first-hand, with Khok Khwaj (Uthai Thani) comparisons taken from Pusit (1986).
